title: Uniformly computable arrays of thin colourings whose thin sets compute the k-th Turing jump
source_title: Ramsey-like theorems for the Schreier barrier

standard_prerequisites.name: Turing functionals, jumps and moduli
standard_prerequisites.statement: The Turing functional Phi_e^X, the k-th Turing jump of the empty set (the halting set for k = 1), the class Delta^0_{k+1}, a uniform modulus of a set (a function dominating its characteristic function's use bound), and the fact that a function dominating a modulus of the k-th jump computes that jump. All of these are used as they stand at source lines 688 and 696 and are not re-proved.
standard_prerequisites.use: The colouring is built from a uniform modulus and the conclusion is the computability of the k-th jump from a thin set.

standard_prerequisites.name: Thin sets for a colouring
standard_prerequisites.statement: For a colouring f from the n-element subsets of the natural numbers into a non-empty set C and a colour c in C, an infinite H is f-thin for c when c is not in f applied to the n-element subsets of H; the article's own definition is retained from source lines 665-667, as is the principle TS^n_k at 675-677.
standard_prerequisites.use: The statement and every step of the proof are phrased as thinness for an explicitly named colour.

standard_prerequisites.name: Finite combinatorics of tuples in an infinite set
standard_prerequisites.statement: An infinite set of natural numbers supplies arbitrarily long increasing tuples, and tuples can be completed beyond any prescribed bound while keeping the first coordinates fixed.
standard_prerequisites.use: Used at source lines 692 and 694 to force the top colour and then to realise any smaller colour.

core_obligations: Build the colourings f_n^k from a uniform modulus g_k of the set of k-th jump: set f_n^k(x_0,...,x_{n-1}) to n-1 when g_k(x_0) <= x_1, and otherwise to the largest i < n-1 with g_k(x_0) > x_{i+1}, and record that Delta^0_{k+1}-indexes for the moduli g_k are found computably and uniformly in k (source lines 688-690).

Show that the top colour n-1 is never the avoided colour of an infinite thin set: for any x_0 in H the set H minus the initial segment up to g_k(x_0) supplies x_1 < ... < x_{n-1}, on which the value is n-1 (source line 692).

Show that an infinite H which is f_n^k-thin for a colour c < n-1 is also thin for the colour n-2: a tuple on which colour n-2 appears forces g_k(x_0) > x_{n-1}, and then completing the tuple beyond g_k(x_0) realises the colour c (source line 694).

Convert thinness for the colour n-2 into the growth bound g_k(x_i) <= x_{i+n-1} for H enumerated as x_0 < x_1 < ..., so that H dominates the modulus g_k and therefore computes the k-th jump, and check that the whole computation is uniform in H, k and n (source line 696).

Assemble the two arrays of Turing indexes e_{n,k} and d_{n,k} so that the statement holds simultaneously for all n, k in the positive integers with n >= 2, which is the uniformity the article needs and which the finite-dimensional result it improves does not provide (source lines 683-685 and 696).

proof_roadmap.step: Take a uniform modulus g_k of the k-th jump with Delta^0_{k+1}-indexes found uniformly, and define f_n^k by comparing x_1 with g_k(x_0).
Rule out the top colour n-1 as an avoided colour, using that an infinite set supplies a long tuple beyond g_k(x_0).
Show that thinness for a colour c < n-1 forces thinness for the colour n-2, by extending a tuple beyond g_k(x_0) to realise c.
Turn thinness for the colour n-2 into g_k(x_i) <= x_{i+n-1}, so that H dominates g_k and computes the k-th jump uniformly.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is Lemma lem:arrays at source lines 683-685: two arrays of Turing indexes must be produced so that the k-th-jump-computable colourings f_n^k from n-element subsets onto n colours exist uniformly in n and k and every infinite f_n^k-thin set computes the k-th jump through the single index d_{n,k}. The colouring at source line 690 encodes a uniform modulus g_k of the k-th jump into a colour by comparing x_1 with g_k(x_0) and otherwise returning the largest i < n-1 with g_k(x_0) > x_{i+1}, and the three steps that follow are each needed: the top colour n-1 is avoided outright (line 692), thinness for any smaller colour c has to be pushed up to the colour n-2 by extending a tuple beyond g_k(x_0) (line 694), and only then does thinness for n-2 give the growth bound g_k(x_i) <= x_{i+n-1} which makes the jump computable from H (line 696). The uniformity in n and k, which the finite-dimensional result this lemma improves does not supply, is what cannot be obtained by quoting that result, and the article says so in the paragraph preceding the lemma.

dedup.scope: Same-source public primary and all five claims already prepared from this source, plus the public identity index, the retired-claims record and the current worklist searched with the object names thin set, uniformly computable colouring, dominating modulus, k-th Turing jump, rainbow and Schreier barrier.

compared.difference: Same source but a different unit: that public item counts the proposition printed at source lines 585-587, which in this fixed v3 source lies inside the authors' iffalse block at 584-626 and is therefore no longer part of the paper; its content is a Weihrauch and Reverse-Mathematics reduction between the exactly-omega-large free set and rainbow principles, not a computability-theoretic construction of uniform colourings.

Counts Theorem ts-omega-computes-omega-jump (source lines 719-721), the single exactly-omega-large thin colouring whose thin sets compute the omega-th jump. lem:arrays is the uniformly indexed finite-dimensional ingredient proved immediately before it (lines 683-697); that theorem is not a premise here, and the uniformity in n and k is exactly what it later consumes.

Counts Theorem fs_red_rt (source lines 419-421), the strong Weihrauch reduction of the exactly-omega-large free set theorem to binary Ramsey; different section, different objects, and no Turing-jump coding.

Counts the computable progressive-barrier halting-code proposition (source lines 1057-1059), a barrier and forcing construction; it never uses a modulus of the k-th jump or thin sets of n-element tuples.

Counts the strong cone avoidance theorem (source lines 1083-1089); cone avoidance asserts that solutions avoid a cone, the opposite direction from the jump-coding conclusion proved here, and its machinery is not used.
Counts the two-bounded-rainbow halting-code proposition for barriers of order type omega to the omega (source lines 905-907); different principle, different construction.

editorial_notes: The counted unit is the article's own Lemma lem:arrays (source lines 683-685) together with the proof that begins on the next line (687-697); the pairing is the ordinary adjacent one.

The sentence that motivates the lemma, at source line 679, contrasts this uniform construction with the non-uniform finite-dimensional result of Dorais et al.; it is not extracted because it carries a citation for which this fixed source supplies no bibliography entry, and its content is recorded here and in the allowed prerequisites instead.

This article numbers all theorem-like environments in one sequence within each section, so the retained definitions print as 4.1 and 4.2 and the counted lemma as 4.3, matching the source's own numbering; the original label lem:arrays is carried in the span metadata.
The authors' iffalse block at source lines 584-626 and the iffalse section at 1307-1376 are not extracted, so no counted unit rests on material the authors removed.
No retained line contains a citation, a figure or an included file.

editorial_scope: One original result: the article's Lemma lem:arrays with its complete author proof, plus the article's own definitions of an f-thin set and of the finite-dimensional Thin Set Theorem. The five claims already counted from this source, in particular the omega-th-jump theorem that later consumes this lemma, are not counted here and are not used as premises.
